subject: Estimation issue with Poisson and inla.posterior.sample

messages.author: d54aba6af40f8c5e
messages.subject: Estimation issue with Poisson and inla.posterior.sample
parts:
Hi,

I'm having an issue with using R-INLA to obtained estimates of linear combinations of counts for Poisson data after the link function has been applied. I have random effects (for groups) but am trying to estimate individual-level averages from a model with random (group) effects. I'm using sampling to estimate the linear combinations after the link function has been applied.

I consistently get upwardly biased results with INLA, while with rstanarm the results are more accurate (though much slower) in this situation. I realize that different priors are being used here, but I am struggling to get INLA to give more accurate estimates. Any help would be appreciated greatly as INLA obviously scales much better than Stan for larger datasets (and I like INLA).

Here's a simplified example:

rm(list=ls())

set.seed(1)
N <- 500
num.grps <- 50
grps <- sample(1:num.grps,N,rep=T)
re <- rnorm(num.grps,sd=1.5)
eta <- -1 + re[grps]
y <- rpois(N,lambda=exp(eta))
dat <- data.frame(y,grps)

f <- y ~ 1 + f(grps)
mod <- inla(f,
            data=dat,
            family="poisson",
            control.predictor=list(link=1),
            control.compute=list(config=TRUE)
            )

get.samp <- function(mod,M=1000) {
    samp <- inla.posterior.sample(M,mod)
    latents <- t(sapply(samp,function(x) x$latent[,1]))
}

samp.preds <- get.samp(mod)[,1:nrow(dat)]
samp <- exp(samp.preds)

vec <- apply(samp,1,mean)
quantile(vec,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975))

## INLA estimates
##      50%     2.5%    97.5%
## 1.374633 1.266518 1.483474

## "Truth" (individual-level)
## mean(dat$y)
## [1] 1.336

require(rstanarm); options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
mod.stan <- stan_glmer(y ~ 1 + (1|grps),
                       data=dat,
                       family=poisson)
samp.stan <- exp(posterior_linpred(mod.stan))
vec <- apply(samp.stan,1,mean)
quantile(vec,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975))

## Stan estimates
##      50%     2.5%    97.5%
## 1.336078 1.241095 1.437824

Hi & thanks for this. Very useful.

Seems to be due to the case that the marginals are (negatively) skewed,
and the sampling does not account for that (assumes its Gaussian). One
of the students works on this problem, and I'll discuss it with him and
come back to you.

Best
H

parts:
Hi,

an update on this issue. correcting for skewness we can improve the
estimates, but the main issue below, is that the default priors used
are different. priors for the intercept and the precision. To check for
bias you need to compare two identical models.

H

messages.author: d54aba6af40f8c5e
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Estimation issue with Poisson and inla.posterior.sample
parts:
Thank you very much for this. My problem is that I consistently get upwardly biased results from INLA here, despite the priors I use.

Please see comparison with JAGS below. I believe the priors are equivalent (though perhaps a bit silly), yet the issue persists.

require(INLA)

rm(list=ls())

set.seed(1)
N <- 500
num.grps <- 50
grps <- sample(1:num.grps,N,rep=T)
re <- rnorm(num.grps,sd=1.5)
eta <- -1 + re[grps]
y <- rpois(N,lambda=exp(eta))
dat <- data.frame(y,grps)

lg.prior <- list(prec = list(prior="loggamma",
                             param=c(0.1,0.1)))
f <- y ~ 1 + f(grps,hyper=lg.prior)

mod <- inla(f,
            data=dat,
            family="poisson",
            control.predictor=list(link=1),

control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
            control.fixed=list(mean.intercept=0,
                               prec.intercept=0.001)
            )

get.samp <- function(mod,M=1000,seed=1) {
    samp <- inla.posterior.sample(M,mod,seed=seed)

latents <- t(sapply(samp,function(x) x$latent[,1]))
}

samp.preds <- get.samp(mod)[,1:nrow(dat)]
samp <- exp(samp.preds)

vec <- apply(samp,1,mean)
quantile(vec,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975))

## INLA estimates
##      50%     2.5%    97.5%

## 1.376197 1.271512 1.483621

## Empirical value (individual-level)
mean(dat$y)
## [1] 1.336

################
### JAGS Way ###
################

require(R2jags)
my.model <- function() {
    for(i in 1:N) {
        y[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])
        log(mu[i]) <- alpha + re[grps[i]]
    }
    for(j in 1:num.grps) {
        re[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau)
    }
    alpha ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    tau ~ dgamma(0.1,0.1)

    sd <- 1/sqrt(tau)
}

require(R2jags)
mod.jags <- jags(data=c("y","grps","N","num.grps"),
                 n.chains=1,
                 n.iter=10000,
                 parameters=c("mu","alpha","sd"),
                 inits=list(list(alpha=1,
                                 re=rep(0,num.grps),
                                 tau=2)),
                 model.file=my.model)$BUGSoutput
mu <- mod.jags$sims.list$mu
vec.jags <- apply(mu,1,mean)
quantile(vec.jags,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975))
##      50%     2.5%    97.5%
## 1.333624 1.235130 1.441453
On Thursday, December 13, 2018 at 9:54:08 PM UTC-8, Helpdesk wrote:

Hi,

an update on this issue. correcting for skewness we can improve the
estimates, but the main issue below, is that the default priors used
are different. priors for the intercept and the precision. To check for
bias you need to compare two identical models.

H
